title: The History of Carrots — The Root That Was Never Orange
fullText: Picture the carrot section at your local grocery store. Rows and rows of bright orange roots, neatly trimmed and bagged, looking like they have always been that way. You would think the carrot has always been orange. It has not. For most of its 5,000year history, the carrot was purple, yellow, white, sometimes even black. The orange carrot you grew up eating, the one sitting in your fridge right now, is only about 500 years old. and the story of how it turned orange involves Dutch [music] politics, wartime propaganda, Walt Disney, and one of the strangest rebranding campaigns in the history of food. The Carrot story starts in a place most people would not expect. Not a farm, not a garden, but a wild hillside in what is now Afghanistan and Iran. About 5,000 years ago, the ancestor of every carrot you have ever eaten was a scraggly, thin, white root growing wild across central Asia and the Persian plateau. [music] If you pulled one out of the ground back then, you would not have recognized it as a carrot. [music] It looked nothing like what we eat today. It was small, forked, covered in fine hairs, incredibly bitter, and so woody you [music] could barely chew it. Imagine pulling a twig out of the dirt and trying to eat it. That is closer to the experience of biting into an ancient wild carrot than anything you would find at a modern supermarket. If you have ever [music] seen a weed called Queen Anne's lace growing along a road or in an open field, you have actually seen this ancestor with your own eyes. Queen Anne's lace, the wild flower with [music] the delicate white umbrella-shaped blooms that grows across North America and Europe, is the same species as the [music] modern carrot. Its scientific name is dorcus corro. If you crush the stem, it smells like carrot. And if you dig up the root during its first year of growth, you will find a small, pale, tough tap [music] routt down there. That little white root is what the original carrot looked like. Every orange carrot at every grocery [music] store in the world descended from something that looks like a roadside weed. The carrot did not start as food. It started as a wild flower. But here is what makes the early history so interesting. The first people to cultivate wild carrots were not growing them for the root at all. They were growing them for the seeds and the leaves. The aromatic seeds were used as a flavoring in food. Something like a rough cousin of cumin or carowway. Herbalists across Persia and Central Asia prized the [music] leaves and roots almost entirely as medicine. They used wild carrot preparations to treat digestive problems, kidney ailments, and urinary infections. Some cultures [music] used it as a mild sweetener because the wild carrot root had a surprisingly high sugar content, second only to beets among root vegetables. In ancient Greece, the physician Dioscorides wrote about wild carrot as a remedy. In parts of Appalachia, wild carrot [music] was used as a folk remedy well into the 19th century. The point is that for thousands of years, the carrot was something you took [music] when you were sick. Nobody was sitting down to a plate of carrots for dinner. This was pharmacy, not cuisine. And that distinction carried forward for centuries. When the cultivated carrot made [music] its way westward into Greece and Rome, the ancient writers who mentioned it were still mostly talking about its medicinal properties. Ply [music] the Elder, the Roman naturalist who lived from 23 to 79 AD, wrote about a root vegetable that historians believe was the carrot. Though even he seemed unsure exactly what he was describing. That confusion was not just ply being careless. It was [music] a problem that lasted for over a thousand years. For the entire classical period and well into the Middle Ages, writers treated carrots and parsnips as basically the same plant. The Roman cookbook attributed to Epicius, which is the most complete surviving manuscript on food from the Imperial Roman [music] era and covers nearly 500 dishes, includes recipes for what [music] it calls kote su pastin, which translates to carrots or parnips. The Romans literally did not care which one you used. As far as their kitchens were concerned, both roots were interchangeable. This seems bizarre to us because a modern carrot and a modern parnip look completely different. One [music] is orange and about 7 in long. The other is pale ivory and can grow up to [music] 3 ft, but that contrast did not exist back then. The early carrots were thin, pale, and woody, and so were the parsnips. Both were white or off-white. [music] Both were root vegetables in the same botanical family. Both tasted earthy and a little bitter. The second century physician Galen tried to formally separate the two by giving the carrot the name Dorcas [music] pastanaka. But even that effort did not fully resolve the confusion. In old English, both vegetables were called by the same word moru. Nobody could tell [music] them apart because there was barely anything to tell apart. There is one story from Roman times worth mentioning on its own though. Emperor Caligula, who ruled from 37 to 41 [music] AD, and whose reputation for extreme and unpredictable behavior is well documented, allegedly ordered the entire Roman Senate [music] to attend a formal banquet where every single dish was made from carrots. The reason, according to the historical accounts, [music] was that Caligula believed carrots had aphrodesiac properties. The ancient Romans and Greeks both associated the carrot with sexual potency, [music] probably because of the roots shape more than anything scientific. Ply [music] himself mentioned this connection. Whether the banquet actually happened is debatable, but the fact that the story exists tells you something [music] about how the carrot was perceived in the ancient world. It was a curiosity, a medicine, sometimes a punchline. It was not yet a staple. The carrot's transformation from wild medicine to serious cultivated [music] crop really gained momentum during the early medieval period. By around the 10th century, farmers in the region [music] spanning from Afghanistan to what is now Turkey were actively growing domesticated varieties and these domesticated carrots had already started changing color. The most common cultivated carrots in this part of the world [music] were deep purple and bright yellow. The purple color came from compounds called [music] anthocyanins, the same pigments that make blueberries dark and give red cabbage its violet hue. [music] The yellow came from carotenoids, a different family of plant pigments that would later become incredibly important to nutrition science. These early domesticated carrots [music] split into two main groups over time. The eastern or Asiatic group was cultivated around the Himalayas and central Asia and tended to produce purple branching roots. [music] The western group grown across the Middle East and into Turkey included yellow and occasionally pale orange varieties. A 2000 BC Egyptian temple drawing appears to depict a purple plant that [music] Egyptologists believe may be a carrot. Both groups were still a long way from the fat, sweet, uniform orange root you buy [music] in a plastic bag, but the raw genetic material was there. Farmers were already selecting for sweeter flavor, bigger roots, [music] and more appealing colors. The carrot was being shaped by human hands generation by generation without anyone calling it genetic engineering. Around 1100 AD, the cultivated carrot was reintroduced to Europe. This is a detail that often surprises people because wild carrots had been growing in Europe for ages. But the wild ones growing in European ditches were still small, bitter, and not worth eating on purpose. The cultivated gardenworthy varieties that [music] could actually produce a root worth putting on a plate came from the east. Arab [music] traders and travelers brought seeds and agricultural knowledge with them along trade routes through Moish Spain and the Mediterranean. And the [music] carrot started appearing in European gardens for the first time as a food crop rather than a weed or a curiosity. This was the moment when Europe [music] first got the domesticated carrot as we would recognize it. And it came in purple and yellow, not orange. By the 1300s, you could find [music] purple and yellow carrots growing in Spain, Italy, France, and eventually the Netherlands and England. The word carrot itself came into English [music] around 1500 borrowed from the French karat which came from the Latin karota which in turn came from the Greek koten. That Greek root probably traces back to a protoindo-uropean word meaning horn or head, a reference to [music] the roots pointed hornlike shape. But even at this point in history, roughly the year [music] 1500, the carrot was still not orange. That detail matters [music] more than it might seem. For about 4,500 years of its cultivated [music] history across dozens of civilizations and continents, the carrot existed in every [music] color except the one we now consider its defining trait. The orange carrot was born in the Netherlands in the late 1500s. Dutch farmers who by this time were among the most skilled and systematic agricultural innovators in Europe began selectively breeding yellow and white carrot varieties. What they were after was practical. They wanted a carrot that tasted sweeter, grew more uniformly, resisted pests better, and produced higher yields. Through careful crossbreeding and selection over many generations, they managed to amplify the beta [music] carotene content in these carrots which gradually shifted the color from pale yellow to a deeper richer [music] orange. Now there is a famous legend attached to this part of the story. It claims that Dutch growers deliberately bred the orange carrot as a patriotic tribute to William of Orange, the leader of the Dutch revolt against Spain and the man widely credited [music] as the founder of the Dutch Republic. It is a great story and it gets repeated everywhere [music] from textbooks to food blogs to documentaries. But according to John Stalachic, the curator of the World Carrot Museum, who has spent years combing through files at the Imperial War Museum, the UK National Archives, [music] and other European collections, there is no documentary evidence that Dutch farmers created [music] the orange carrots specifically to honor the royal family. The connection to the house of orange likely came after the fact. Dutch horiculturists probably found a mutant orange colored variety among their yellow [music] and white carrots, recognized that it was sweeter and more appealing and selectively [music] breded for those qualities. The patriotic origin story was attached later when the carrot's color happened to match the national symbol. Regardless of the motivation, the result was the same. Two specific Dutch varieties called long orange and [music] early scarlet horn became the genetic foundation for almost every orange carrot grown in [music] the western world. A 2023 study actually mapped the exact genetic pathways that pump up alpha and beta carotene in what scientists [music] call western carrots and found that Dutch breeders were accidentally fixing [music] these precise biological mechanisms centuries before anyone understood the science. They did not need to understand genetics. They just knew a good carrot [music] when they saw one. These varieties spread across Europe through Dutch trade networks which stretched from the East Indies to the Americas and touched nearly every major port in between. Within a few generations, the orange carrot had largely [music] replaced its purple and yellow ancestors in European gardens and markets. The reasons were straightforward [music] enough. Orange carrots were sweeter and less bitter than their purple and yellow [music] cousins. They grew in more uniform shapes, which made harvesting and selling them much [music] easier. And there was one more advantage that rarely gets discussed. Purple carrots, when cooked, tended to bleed a dark blue or violet dye into whatever dish they were part of. That staining made food look unappetizing. Orange carrots [music] kept their color during cooking and did not discolor the rest of the meal. For farmers trying to [music] sell produce at market and for cooks trying to make a dish look appealing, that practical difference mattered as much [music] as the taste. By the 1700s, the orange carrot had become the standard across most of [music] Europe. And then in 1831, a German chemist named Hinrich Wilhelm Ferdinand Vakenroa isolated a yellow orange pigment from carrot juice extracts at the pharmaceutical institute in Jenna. He named it keratin [music] from the Latin word for carrot carrot. We now call it beta carotene. This was the molecule responsible [music] for the carrot's orange color and it would later turn out to be one of the most nutritionally significant compounds [music] ever identified in the plant world. When scientists discovered vitamin A in 1913, [music] they realized that dietary beta carotene from plants could prevent vitamin [music] A deficiency in humans. The carrot, which had spent most of its history as a folk medicine prescribed by [music] herbalists who could not have explained why it worked, turned out to contain genuine medical value after all, just not [music] the kind the ancients had in mind when they were using it as an aphrodesiac. [music] That connection between carrots and health, between betaarotene and eyesight specifically set the stage for one of the most successful and persistent propaganda campaigns in modern history. And to understand how it happened, you need to go to England in 1940. When World War II broke out, the British Royal Air Force had a secret weapon. In 1939, they deployed a new technology called airborne interception radar, which allowed fighter pilots to detect incoming German bombers at night before they even reached the English Channel. The technology was classified, [music] and the British government desperately needed to keep it that way. But there was a problem. [music] RAF night fighters were suddenly shooting down German planes at an unprecedented rate, and both the press and the public were starting to ask how they were doing it. The pilots needed a public explanation for their success that had nothing to do with radar. Enter John Cunningham. He was a 23-year-old former test pilot who had never flown a combat mission before the war started. Once radar equipped Bristol bow fighters [music] entered service, Cunningham became devastatingly effective at night interceptions. The British press gave him the nickname Cat's eyes [music] Cunningham, and the government ran with it. They told newspapers that his extraordinary night vision came from eating enormous quantities of carrots. His diet, [music] they claimed, was what allowed him to spot German bombers in pitch darkness. The radar technology guiding his every move went completely unmentioned. The propaganda quickly expanded far beyond a simple cover story for one pilot. The British Ministry of Food saw a much [music] bigger opportunity. Before the war, Britain imported about 70% of its food. Once German yubot began blockading supply ships in the Atlantic, staples like sugar, bacon, and butter became scarce. Rationing [music] was introduced in 1940, but carrots could be grown locally in backyard [music] victory gardens. They were cheap, hardy, and easy to cultivate in [music] the British climate. The government needed the public to eat far more of them. So, the Ministry of Food launched a massive [music] advertising campaign. They created a cartoon mascot called Dr. Carrot, [music] a cheerful anthropomorphic carrot character wearing a top hat, spats, and spectacles. and carrying [music] a medical bag labeled Vite. Alongside him was a companion character called Potato [music] Pete. Posters went up across the country. BBC radio broadcasts promoted carrot recipes. The ministry published pamphlets with instructions for making carrot [music] curry, carrot jam, carrot fudge, and a particularly grim sounding vegetable juice drink called carolade, which mixed carrot juice with Rutabbaker. The campaign got so big that even Walt Disney [music] got involved. Lord Walton, the British Minister of Food, sent Disney a telegram asking for more carrot mascots to help [music] with the effort. A Disney cartoonist named Hank Porter designed an entire fictional family based on Dr. Carrot, [music] Cary George, Pop Carrot, and Claraara Carrot. The British government [music] ultimately decided not to distribute the Disney characters widely because officials felt they were too American in style. But the fact that Disney was designing carrot propaganda during a world war tells you how seriously Britain took this initiative. And the campaign worked arguably too well. By 1942, Britain had accumulated a surplus of 100,000 tons [music] of carrots. The government literally had more carrots than it knew what to do with, [music] and it had to figure out how to get people to consume even more of them. The carrots help you see in the dark messaging, which had started as a military cover story for Radar, [music] became the primary marketing angle for the entire surplus. The question historians still debate is whether the Germans actually fell for the carrot story. There is no definitive evidence that Luftvafa intelligence seriously believed diet was the reason British pilots were intercepting them. The Germans were skeptical, [music] but there are scattered anecdotal accounts of German squadrons ordering extra carrots for their own pilots just in case. The Germans did eventually develop their own airborne radar. And some historians have pointed [music] out that by the time the carrot propaganda really ramped up in 1942, the Germans had already recovered a [music] downed British radar set and knew the technology existed. So the carrot [music] story may have been less about fooling the enemy and more about motivating the home front to eat [music] a vegetable they had too much of. Either way, the effect on the British and eventually the American public was permanent. The idea [music] that carrots improve your eyesight entered popular culture during the war and never left. Your grandmother probably told you to eat your carrots so you could see better. She believed it because her mother believed it [music] and her mother believed it because the British government told her so in 1941. The science behind the claim is real but stretched [music] far beyond its actual meaning. Carrots do contain betaarotene which your body converts into vitamin A. Vitamin A is genuinely necessary for healthy vision. If you have a vitamin A deficiency, [music] which causes a condition called night blindness, eating carrots will help restore your eyesight to normal levels. But if your vitamin A levels are already fine, eating extra carrots [music] will not sharpen your vision. It will not let you see in the dark. It will not make you a better pilot. Eat too many carrots in fact and the excess beta carotene can actually turn your skin yellow orange a harmless condition called keratenemia. [music] As one optometric physician put it, when patients ask about carrots, he tells them that Popey is more knowledgeable about [music] eye health than Bugs Bunny. Speaking of Bugs Bunny, the carrot munching rabbit was himself a product of wartime culture. Warner Brothers introduced the character during the same years that carrot propaganda was reaching [music] its peak. The animators reportedly based his carrot eating habit on a scene from the 1934 film [music] It Happened One Night, where Clark Gable peels and eats a carrot while talking fast. The image of [music] a wisecracking rabbit constantly chewing on a carrot embedded itself in American culture so deeply that many [music] people now think of carrots as a natural rabbit food. In reality, carrots are [music] too sweet for most rabbits digestive systems and should not be a regular part of their diet. Veterinarians say so constantly, and [music] pet owners constantly ignore them because the Bugs Bunny image is just that strong. Decades of cartoons overrode the actual biology. That association, [music] like the night vision claim, was manufactured, not by a government this time, but by an animation studio in Hollywood. Today, the carrot is one of the most widely produced vegetables on the planet. In 2024, global production of carrots [music] and turnips combined hit roughly 45 million tons. China is the largest producer by a wide margin, growing about 42% of the global [music] supply, which works out to somewhere around 18 to 20 million tons per year. Usuzbekiststan comes in a distant [music] second at about 4 million tons, followed by the United States at about 1.4 million tons with 85% of the American carrot crop grown in California. The average American eats between 8 [music] and 9 lb of carrots every year. The carrot has been described as America's most [music] trusted vegetable by food industry publications, partly because it has never been involved in the kind [music] of large-scale contamination incidents that have affected crops like lettuce and spinach. But the dominance of the orange carrot has started to shift at least slightly. Over the past couple of decades, [music] farmers and food enthusiasts have been rediscovering the heirloom varieties that dominated for thousands of years before the Dutch changed everything. You can now find [music] purple, red, yellow, and white carrots at farmers markets and some specialty grocery stores. Purple carrots in particular have attracted [music] attention because they contain high levels of anthocyanins, the same antioxidant compounds that make blueberries [music] and asai berries popular with healthconscious consumers. The Vegetable Improvement Center at Texas A and M University developed a carrot with purple skin and orange flesh that is specifically bred to be nutrientdense. These varieties are not novelties [music] or gimmicks. They are the carrot's original identity, making a commercial comeback [music] after five centuries in the shadow of the Dutch orange. And there is something worth sitting with in that fact. The purple carrot feels exotic to us. It shows up on restaurant [music] menus as a specialty item. You pay more for it at the farmers market, but it is the original version. The orange carrot is the newcomer. The orange variety is a few centuries old at most. A product of selective breeding in a small corner of northern Europe. We just happen to live in the narrow window of history where orange became the default. So we treat everything else as the exception. The carrot's journey is a reminder that the foods we think of as natural and eternal [music] have been shaped by human choices at every turn. Wild carrots [music] were white and bitter and medicinal. Early farmers turned them purple and yellow. The Dutch turned them orange. The British turned them into [music] war propaganda. Disney turned them into a cartoon prop. Warner Brothers made them the signature snack of one of the most famous animated characters ever created. Scientists named one of the most important nutritional compounds in existence after them. And through all of it, the carrot just kept growing, adapting to whatever role humans needed it to play. The word carrot itself comes from a Greek word meaning horn, a reference to its pointed shape. Keratene, the pigment that makes it orange, literally means from the carrot. The molecule was named after the vegetable. That is how central this root has become to our lives and our science. We did [music] not just eat it. We named our chemistry after it. 5,000 years from wild weed to global staple. Thousands of years as medicine before anyone thought to eat it for dinner. Centuries spent in purple before anyone saw it in orange. A world war where the real weapon was radar, [music] but the cover story was root vegetables. And now 45 million tons of it pulled from the earth every single year. Grown on every populated continent in a color that would have confused any farmer who cultivated carrots before the 1500s. The carrot has been through more reinventions than most companies [music] manage in their entire existence. And it is still going, still adapting, still being bred into new shapes and colors for new [music] markets and new generations of people who have no idea how strange the carrot's backstory really is. The next [music] time you pick up a bag of carrots at the store, you are holding a 5,000-year-old science experiment, [music] a wartime propaganda tool, and one of the most successfully rebranded products in history. All disguised [music] as a vegetable. If you enjoyed this video, hit subscribe and leave a comment telling us which part of [music] the carrot's history surprised you the most.
